summary: Almost everything out here arrived as a named subdivision, and the record is the city taking the names in. In 1917 the streets of Westwood Park — Valdez Avenue, Westwood Drive, Wildwood Way, Kenwood Way — were declared open public streets straight off the developer's map, and St. Francis Wood, West Portal Park and Forest Hill came the same way. St. Francis Circle was opened in 1918 out of a piece of land a hundred and fifty-five feet across where five roads met, and Junipero Serra Boulevard was paved from Ocean Avenue to the county line for fifty thousand dollars. Twice in ten days in March 1910 the San Francisco Motor Club was allowed to race cars up Nineteenth Avenue from Sloat Boulevard to the top of the hill. Between the tracts the Board spent thirty years re-setting grades on Flood, Staples, Hearst and Mangels avenues and arguing with contractors about who would finish. The tracts are still being cut finer — a single-family lot on Congo Street proposed for four in 2020, two of them undersized. The ground still moves: a landslide between Casitas Avenue and Miraloma Drive in January 2016 left the city settling claims worth up to five million dollars. Lately it has mostly been naming what is already standing — the Cowell House on San Marcos Avenue in 2015, the El Rey Theater on Ocean Avenue in 2017, the Westwood Park entrance pillars in 2023, the Gregangelo Museum on San Leandro Way in 2024 — while doing the whole thing over again at the Balboa Reservoir, sold to a developer in 2020 and given four new street names in 2023: Diego Lane, Loquat Lane, Meyer Lane and Wisteria Lane.
